summary: Defines text/enriched, a MIME type for email text with simple formatting such as bold and italic, marked up with tags. It was meant to be easy for programs to read and still readable as plain text. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: text/enriched is a MIME text format that adds simple formatting commands to email. A reader that does not support a command can ignore it and still display the text.

questions: how to format email text in mime
how does text/enriched mark bold text
how are line breaks handled in text/enriched
subtitle: A small set of formatting commands for enriched text in MIME email.

tldr.problem: Plain text does not express common formatting, while the RFC judged richer markup formats too complex or insufficiently supported for its purpose.
tldr.mechanism: The text/enriched subtype places simple formatting commands in angle brackets and defines rules for nesting commands and interpreting line breaks.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1896 is Informational, obsoletes RFC 1523 and RFC 1563, and describes text/enriched as a short-term format until other MIME text-formatting types are developed and deployed.

today: RFC 1896 is an Informational RFC published in February 1996. It obsoletes RFC 1523 and RFC 1563; the RFC describes text/enriched as intended for short-term use.

sections.title: Goals of text/enriched
sections.content:
text/enriched is a MIME subtype for simple formatted text. The RFC aims for syntax that is easy to parse, extensible, readable when displayed without MIME formatting, and limited enough to encourage consistent rendering.

The document presents it as a minor revision of earlier text/enriched descriptions and a short-term approach until other MIME text-formatting types are developed and deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: The format adds a small number of text styles without requiring a reader to understand a complex markup language. If formatting is unavailable, the words remain readable.

sections.title: Syntax and Line Breaks
sections.content:
Text uses one character set, US-ASCII by default. The less-than sign begins a formatting command; a literal less-than sign is written as two consecutive less-than signs.

Commands use opening and closing forms and must be balanced. An isolated CRLF becomes a space, while multiple consecutive CRLF pairs represent line breaks according to the rules in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Angle-bracket commands mark formatting. A single line break is treated as a space, while repeated line breaks create paragraph spacing.

sections.title: Formatting Commands
sections.content:
The RFC defines font commands such as bold, italic, underline, fixed-width, color, and size changes. It also defines layout commands for alignment, indentation, and preserving line breaks, as well as commands for quoted excerpts and language labels.

Implementations may support different commands. An unrecognized command should not prevent the text from being displayed, and private extensions can use names beginning with X-.
sections.plainLanguage: Commands can change how text looks or how lines are arranged. A mail reader can ignore commands it does not recognize and still show the text.

sections.title: Character Sets and Minimal Support
sections.content:
The charset parameter can identify a character set for the text. Formatting commands themselves use ASCII syntax, and formatting does not continue across MIME body-part boundaries.

A minimal reader can display the content by removing formatting commands, handling escaped less-than signs, and applying the specified line-break rules. More capable readers can render the supported formatting.
sections.plainLanguage: The message identifies its character set, and formatting commands are separate from the text they affect. Even a basic reader can remove the commands and show the remaining words.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that the mechanism raises no security issues.

It provides no further security analysis in this section.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC states that text/enriched raises no security issues. It does not provide a further security analysis.
